# Job Chapter 17 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 422r–422v

---

**1** "My spirit is crushed. My days are snuffed out. The grave is all that is left for me.

**2** I am surrounded by mockers. I lie awake staring at their insults.

**3** God, put up a guarantee for me yourself! Who else would go to bat for me?

**4** You have shut their minds to understanding — so surely you will not let them win this argument.

**5** If a man betrays his friends for profit, his own children will pay the price.

**6** God has made me a joke among the nations. People spit in my face.

**7** My eyes are worn out from grief. My whole body is wasting to a shadow.

**8** Decent people are shocked by what has happened to me. The innocent are outraged at the godless.

**9** Yet the righteous still hold their course, and those with clean hands grow stronger.

**10** But as for all of you — go ahead, try again. I will not find a single wise person among you.

**11** My days are over. My plans have been ripped apart — everything my heart desired.

**12** These friends of mine turn night into day. 'Look, the light is coming!' they say — when all around me is darkness.

**13** If the only home I can hope for is the grave, if I make my bed in the dark,

**14** if I call out to the pit, 'You are my father!' and to the maggot, 'Mother! Sister!' —

**15** then where is my hope? Can anyone see any hope for me?

**16** Will hope go down with me to the gates of death? Will we descend together into the dust?"

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Family of death (v.14):** This is one of the most disturbing images in the Bible. Job has lost his children, his wife has told him to curse God and die, and his friends have become his accusers. With every human relationship severed, Job acknowledges the only family he has left: the grave is his father, the worm is his mother and sister. The intimacy of the language makes it devastating — these are not abstract metaphors but the tender words of kinship applied to decay.

**The righteous paradox (vv.8-9):** These verses puzzle commentators because they seem to assert conventional piety in the middle of Job's despair. The best reading may be ironic — or it may be Job's defiant insistence that integrity matters even when it changes nothing. The righteous hold their course even in the face of what has happened to Job. Whether this is comfort or accusation depends entirely on tone, which the Hebrew does not specify.

**The death of hope (vv.15-16):** The chapter ends not with a statement but with questions — and the questions are rhetorical. Hope cannot follow Job into Sheol. It dies at the threshold of the grave. This is the lowest point of the second cycle.

*— PNEUMA*
